title: The first album and Phil Stein's portrait
summary: Moore explains his album 'Pow Wow Jazz Band', funded with Phil Stein, recorded at the Village Vanguard.

bands.name: Big Chief Moore's Pow Wow Jazz Band

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well, when you finally put out these recordings, your first one was "Big Chief Moore's Pow Wow Jazz Band," with Ed Polger on clarinet, Dick Wellstood on piano, Gene Ramey bass and Jack Williams on drums and that was recorded in 1973 and you've got some old favorites on there, of course, like "Wabash Blues," "St. Louis Blues," "Some Day You'll be Sorry."
Yes, I'll tell you the story of how that album came about. One day I was playing in

a place here in by the name of the Old Banjo and they had jam sessions there and one time I sat in with the band and my rendition of "Jadda" brought tears to a gentleman by the name of Phil Stein. He had his wife with him and I didn't know who Phil Stein was until the set was over and he asked me to come sit at a table with him. So Phil Stein says to me, "Could I do your portrait?" I said, "Sure, you can do my portrait." And I thought he was kidding, I didn't know if he was serious or not. "I tell you what, you come to my house and I'll do your portrait. I loved the way you did 'Jadda.' I never cried before listening to 'Jadda.' Your playing it and singing it. Come to my house, here's my address."

So to make a long story short, I went to his house and I brought my horn, wore a dark suit, and he took my pictures. "I thought you were going to do my portrait." He said, "I have to take pictures first." He took them in color.
So Phil Stein was going to take your picture.
Yeah, he took about a dozen pictures at all angles and he showed me around his studio, he was a sculptor, at least he had portraits

of famous other musicians and also he seemed to like traditional jazz musicians. He's got pictures of Bechet, portraits. So he said to me, "Sit down, I will call you when it's ready." So in the space of about one week, he called me and said, "Your portrait is ready, come on by." So I went to the studio. There it was on a stand, that was wonderful.
It's also on the cover of this.

The album cover. So I said to myself, I wonder how much this guy is going to charge. He said, "It's all yours." The next thing I must do, "Wouldn't you like to make an album?" I said, "Who don't? Sure I want to make an album." "I tell you what we could do. We could put up some money -- I could put up some money -- I said, how much would it take about?" "It would take about $3,000." So he put up some money, I put up some money and my sister put up some money and his sister happens to be the wife of Max Gordon who owns the Village Vanguard and so I put in about seven, eight hundred dollars, somebody put this and somebody that. Low and behold we made the album in the Village Vanguard and my wife and some of the wives came by and we made a big lunch in between the recordings sessions and Max Gordon gave
